title: Warning the witnesses (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)
hookLine: witnesses in capital cases were told that one life is a whole world

cards: The witnesses are brought into the room. A life may depend on what they're about to say. So the court doesn't start with questions.
It starts with a speech. The Mishnah, in the tractate Sanhedrin, gives it almost line by line, and it's surprising. It doesn't quote a penalty for lying.
It tells a story about the first human being, and about coins.

teach.b: Warning the witnesses. You met part of this speech back in year one; today, see the court put it to work. It moves in four steps.
First, the court names the easy mistakes. Perhaps you're speaking from guesswork. Perhaps from hearsay, one witness repeating another, or from someone you trust.
None of that is testimony. Second, the weight. A money case can be repaired with money.
A life case can't. The court points to Cain, and to God's words to him, in the old JPS translation: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground."
In Hebrew, the Mishnah notes, the word is plural: bloods.

teach.h: BLOODS: THE CHILDREN WHO WOULD HAVE BEEN.
teach.b: His blood, and the blood of every child he would have had. Third, the line people still repeat.

Only a single human being was created at the start, to teach that whoever destroys one life is counted as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever sustains one life, as if they sustained a whole world.

teach.h: ONE SEAL, AND NO TWO ALIKE.
teach.b: A person stamps many coins from one seal, and they all come out alike. But every human being is stamped from the seal of the first human, and not one is like another.
So each person must be able to say: the world was created for my sake. A witness is about to describe one person. The court wants them to see, first, that they're describing a world.

how: Jews study Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 as part of the Talmud's order of damages, and its line about saving one life as saving a whole world is quoted in Jewish teaching, memorials and ethics.

s: 'one life is a whole world' began as a saying about charity
in the Mishnah it is part of the warning given to witnesses in a life-and-death case.
the Mishnah reads Cain's story as 'bloods', plural
his brother's blood, and the blood of the children who would have been born.
a witness could repeat what someone trustworthy told them
the warning rules out guesswork and hearsay, even from someone you trust.

games.q: you're a witness. you didn't see it yourself, but someone you trust told you exactly what happened. what does the court tell you before you speak?
o: repeat it. a trustworthy source is enough.
hearsay, even from someone trustworthy, isn't testimony.
say it, but mention it's secondhand.
games.why: the Mishnah's warning names guesswork, hearsay and 'from a trustworthy person' as things a witness must not offer. only what you saw.

practice: Bring to mind someone you might talk about today who won't be in the room, and one thing you'd likely say. Ask the court's questions: did I see this, or only hear it, and would I say it the same way with them sitting here?
Then remember the coin: there's no one else stamped quite like them.

wordCard.voice: Warning the witnesses. The Mishnah's speech before testimony in a life case: one life is a whole world. Today's word, and the close of a week that ran from the chained woman through damages, lost and found, the cloak and the court.

carryVoice: Your line: a whole world. Every person you describe is one of a kind. That's today, done.
